display_title: Official Review of Paper2639 by Reviewer BP8R

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper solves the problem of dialog state tracking in the setting of multimodality. It developed DVD-DST, a synthetic video-grounded dialogue benchmark with annotations of multimodal dialogue states, designed a transformer-based model VDTN for the task, and demonstrated the performance in a response prediction task using the decoded states.
content.main_review:
Strengths: 
1. Multimodal Dialog State Tracking is an important problem to solve with increasing numbers of papers on multimodality in the research community.
2. The VDTN model structure seems reasonable by encoding the information of both visual knowledge and dialog history knowledge using one transformer network.
3. Both the experiments comparing baseline systems on the DVD-DST dataset and the ablation study seem good to me. 

Weakness: 
1. The definition of MM-DST is relatively straightforward for researchers working on DST. I do not consider it a significant contribution.
2. There are several works associated with Multi-modal dialogs (e.g.,  https://arxiv.org/pdf/2007.09903.pdf,  https://arxiv.org/pdf/1911.07928.pdf). I would suggest the authors adding more content elaborating on the differences.
3. Since the benchmark is synthetic based on the generation procedure of DVD. I would suggest the authors elaborating on the quality of the datasets. Otherwise, it is not straightforward to check the performance of the VDTN model.
4. The baselines are not necessarily the best DSTs as of now (check  https://github.com/budzianowski/multiwoz Dialog State Tracking). Adding comparisons with more SOTA DST models should help illustrate the model performance, especially that the current benchmark is new and synthetic.

Thanks for the authors' response. I will keep my original assessment.

On the other hand, there are multiple weaknesses, as mentioned above.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper2639 by Reviewer BP8R

content.title: Response to Reviewer BP8R (part 1)
content.comment:
We would like to thank the reviewer BP8R for the valuable and detailed feedback. We are delighted that the reviewer found our paper well-written and “aiming to push the frontier of multimodal dialogue state tracking”, given current tasks are primarily text-based. Please find below our response: 

>Concern #1: “The definition of MM-DST is relatively straightforward for researchers working on DST.”

We would like to argue that the definition of MM-DST is significantly different from conventional DST by the extension of single-object to multi-object tracking. Conventional DST is limited to only a single entity (e.g. restaurant) per dialogue per domain. We noted there exists DST work that extends from a single domain to multiple domains (e.g. [1]) and hence, multiple entities per dialogue. However, we argue that extending DST from a single object to multiple objects within a single domain (e.g. DVD video domain) is much harder. It is obvious that the semantic variance between in-domain objects (e.g. red vs. blue cube) is smaller than the semantic variance between cross-domain objects (restaurant A vs. taxi B). Therefore, tracking these in-domain objects in a dialogue context in a multimodal DST is inherently more difficult. 

Moreover, as mentioned in our response to Reviewer NrrC and our revised paper in Section 2, our definition of multimodal DST complements current lines of dialogue research while closely modeling capacities found in humans. We believe that the current definition of DST will bring about interesting development to multimodal dialogue systems and improve their usability in the real world.

*[1] Budzianowski et al. (2018).   MultiWOZ - a large-scale multi-domain Wizard-of-Oz datasetfor task-oriented dialogue modelling. In EMNLP.*

>Concern #2: “There are several works associated with Multi-modal dialogs”

Thank you very much for suggesting these related papers! We carefully reviewed these papers (+ a concurrent paper) below and added the discussion in our paper in Appendix A.3. 

In [1], however, we are not convinced that a dialogue state tracking task is a focus, or correctly defined, in this paper. The reported results are exclusively for response prediction. Please let us know if we are wrong. 

In [2], we noted that some form of object tracking is introduced throughout dialogue turns.
The tracking module is used to decide which object the dialogue centers around. This method extends to multi-object tracking but the objects are only limited within static images, and there is no recurring information state (object attributes) maintained at each turn. Compared to our work, their tracking module only requires object identity as a single-slot state from turn to turn.

Almost concurrent to our work, we noted [3] which formally, though very briefly, focuses on multimodal DST. However, the work is limited to the task-oriented domain, and each dialogue is only limited to a single goal-driven object in a synthetic image. While this definition is useful in the task-oriented dialogue domain, it does not account for the DST of multiple visual objects as defined in our work. Moreover, the scope of our work is towards visually-grounded dialogues rather than in the task-oriented paradigm.


*[1] Mou, X., Sigouin, B., Steenstra, I., & Su, H. (2020). Multimodal dialogue state tracking by qa approach with data augmentation. arXiv preprint.*

*[2] Pang, W., & Wang, X. (2020, April). Visual dialogue state tracking for question generation. In AAAI.*

*[3] Kottur, S., Moon, S., Geramifard, A., & Damavandi, B. (2021). SIMMC 2.0: A Task-oriented Dialog Dataset for Immersive Multimodal Conversations. In EMNLP.*

replying_to: Replying to Response to Reviewer BP8R (part 1)

content.title: Response to Reviewer BP8R (part 2)
content.comment:
> Concern #3: “I would suggest the authors elaborating on the quality of the datasets.”

Thank you for your comment. This comment overlaps Concern #2 of reviewer NrrC. We provide our response below and revise the paper in Section 4 ("DVD-DST Benchmark"). 

To study such multimodal DST tasks as defined in this paper, there are not many available suitable benchmarks. The closest possible studies to our task is [1] and [2] but each contains their own shortfalls. In existing popular benchmarks of multimodal dialogues such as VisDial, we observe that a large number of data samples contain strong distribution bias in dialogue context, in which dialogue agents can simply ignore the whole dialogue and rely on image-only features  [3], or annotation bias, in which the causal link connecting dialogue history and current turn question is actually harmful [4]. These biases would obviate the need for a dialogue state in such benchmarks. 

We found that using DVD dialogues can address both biases. The dialogues are grounded on videos from CATER [5] which contain visually simple yet highly varied objects. The dialogues in DVD are synthetically designed with both short-term and long-term object references. These specifications remove the annotation bias in terms of object appearances in visual context and cross-turn dependencies in dialogue context. Moreover, as shown by our results in Table 1, models with access to videos only (RNN(V)) do not perform as well as models with access to dialogue only (RNN(D)). This indicates minimal distribution bias in dialogue context and models can generalize better by relying on dialogue features. 

We also want to highlight that like other synthetic benchmarks such as CLEVR in VQA, we want to use DVD in this work as a test bed to study and design better multimodal dialogue systems. We do not intend to use it to train practical systems for deployment. The DVD benchmark should be used to supplement real-world video-grounded dialogue datasets.

*[1] Pang, W., & Wang, X. (2020). Visual dialogue state tracking for question generation. In AAAI.*

*[2] Kottur, S., Moon, S., Geramifard, A., & Damavandi, B. (2021). SIMMC 2.0: A Task-oriented Dialog Dataset for Immersive Multimodal Conversations. In EMNLP.*

*[3] Kim, H., Tan, H., & Bansal, M. (2020). Modality-balanced models for visual dialogue. In AAAI.*

*[4] Qi, J., Niu, Y., Huang, J., & Zhang, H. (2020). Two causal principles for improving visual dialog. In CVPR.*

*[5] Girdhar, R., & Ramanan, D. (2020). CATER: A diagnostic dataset for Compositional Actions and TEmporal Reasoning. In ICLR.*

>Concern #4: “Adding comparisons with more SOTA DST models should help illustrate the model performance, especially that the current benchmark is new and synthetic.”

Thank you very much for your concern. Indeed, there exist new SOTA models from the unimodal DST research. We will try to add more experiment results and compare them with our models. However, we want to note that not all methods can be trivially applied or relevant in our task. For example, recent SOTA [1] and [2] rely on data-augmentation techniques to improve dialogue context data to address data distribution bias in the MultiWOZ benchmark. However, we do not expect this bias to be strongly present in the DVD-DST benchmark. 

*[1] Li, S., Yavuz, S., Hashimoto, K., Li, J., Niu, T., Rajani, N., ... & Xiong, C. (2021). Coco: Controllable counterfactuals for evaluating dialogue state trackers. In ICLR.*

*[2] Dai, Y., Li, H., Li, Y., Sun, J., Huang, F., Si, L., & Zhu, X. (2021). Preview, Attend and Review: Schema-Aware Curriculum Learning for Multi-Domain Dialog State Tracking. In ACL.*

display_title: Official Review of Paper2639 by Reviewer Sqbw

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper introduced a multimodal dialogue state tracking task that can track visual objects and their attributes mentioned in dialogues and provided a synthetic benchmark for it. It also designed a neural network model for object-level representation learning and multimodal interaction and achieved large performance gains compared to conventional DST models.
content.main_review:
--------------Update--------------------
* There exists another paper "SIMMC 2.0: A Task-oriented Dialog Dataset for Immersive Multimodal Conversations" https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.08667, which is a multi-modal task-oriented dialogue dataset and has rich annotations. This paper is first on arxiv in 8 Apr 2021 and has a Multi-modal DST task. Given that, the current paper's novelty and contribution are significantly weakened. 
----------------------------------
Strengths
* This paper introduced a multi-modal DST task combining video with dialogue text data and also provides a synthetic multimodal DST benchmark.

Weakness
* The motivation to introduce multi-modal DST is unclear to me. The purpose of the traditional DST components in task-oriented dialogue systems is to track users' goals, e.g. restaurant-name, -price, -people etc, which are used to query knowledge base (database), and the query results are used for response generation. However, I don't realize the real-world value to track visual objects in task-oriented systems. The authors may consider clarifying their motivations. 
* The proposed neural network is not quite novel. For example, using a decoder to recover visual representations in a self-supervised learning task to improve video representation learning is not a novel objective function. There exist lots of similar techniques. Wu et al [1] use dialogue history and dialogue state to recover user utterance to improve representation learning. 

[1] Wu et al. Improving Limited Labeled Dialogue State Tracking with Self-Supervision. Findings of EMNLP 2020
content.summary_of_the_review: Although this paper provides a synthetic multi-modal DST benchmark and a neural network to deal with this task, this task itself is not clearly motivated and is far from real-world scenarios, and the proposed neural network is also not quite novel. I think this paper's contribution to the dialogue research community is small and inclined to reject it.

content.title: Response to Reviewer Sqbw
content.comment:
We want to thank the reviewer Sqbw for the valuable feedback. We are glad that the reviewer found some novelty in our multimodal DST task and benchmark. Please find below our response: 

>Concern #1: “I don't realize the real-world value to track visual objects in task-oriented systems”

We want to clarify that our work is not aimed to track visual objects in task-oriented systems but rather in multimodal visually grounded systems. Our motivation is to bring dialogue agents from unimodal to multimodal world, where we leverage the concept of dialogue state tracking from task-oriented dialogue domains. As we mentioned in our response to reviewer NrrC (and revised paper in Section 2), prior studies show that humans are able to perceive the world in scenes, maintaining temporal stability of object representations through time. We want to incorporate this capacity into dialogue agents through the multimodal DST task. 

Moreover, our experiment results in Table 5 show the benefit of using dialogue state predictions to facilitate a response prediction task. While we experimented with a naive integration approach, note that there are more sophisticated integration methods, e.g. symbolic reasoning in the image domain [1], which essentially transforms visual scenes into a knowledge base. In this paradigm, the usability of multimodal DST is very much similar to unimodal DST: to query visual objects and the results are used to support response prediction. 

*[1] Yi, K., Wu, J., Gan, C., Torralba, A., Kohli, P., & Tenenbaum, J. B. (2018). Neural-symbolic vqa: Disentangling reasoning from vision and language understanding. In NeurIPS.*

> Concern #2: “The proposed neural network is not quite novel” 

We respectfully disagree, especially with the reviewer’s comparison of our work with [1]. We think the two papers have completely different goals and the techniques are used in very different ways. While [1] focuses on unimodal DST with constrained resources, we focus on multimodal DST in visually grounded dialogues. [1] perturbed a dialogue context multiple times by masking random words and train models to maintain latent consistency across different perturbed samples.  Instead, we focus on masking visual object/ segment representations (rather than random words), and training models to recover these representations based on their contextual features. 

We would appreciate it if the reviewer can provide more specific related work that might raise novelty concern of our models. 

*[1] Wu et al. Improving Limited Labeled Dialogue State Tracking with Self-Supervision. Findings of EMNLP 2020.*

content.title: Response to Reviewer Sqbw's Update Comment
content.comment:
> There exists another paper "SIMMC 2.0: A Task-oriented Dialog Dataset for Immersive Multimodal Conversations" https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.08667, which is a multi-modal task-oriented dialogue dataset and has rich annotations. This paper is first on arxiv in 8 Apr 2021 and has a Multi-modal DST task. Given that, the current paper's novelty and contribution are significantly weakened.

Thank you for suggesting this paper [1]! We actually already reviewed and included this paper as part of our response to Reviewer BP8R's Concern #3 on 19 Nov (and also revised in our paper in Appendix A.3). 

As we reviewed the paper carefully, we noticed this paper is of a relevant topic. However, we noticed that the paper attends only very briefly on the topic of multimodal DST. The work is limited to the task-oriented domain, and each dialogue is only limited to a single goal-driven object in a synthetic image (i.e. each dialogue state is used to track user intent and retrieve a single visual object). While this definition is useful in the task-oriented dialogue domain, it does not account for the DST of multiple visual objects as defined in our work. Moreover, the scope of our work is towards visually-grounded dialogues rather than in the task-oriented paradigm. In the visually-grounded dialogue domain, a dialogue state definition for a single object per dialogue is significantly insufficient to deal with the type of contextual reasoning required. Finally, while [1] was first on arxiv in April 2021, it is only published recently in the EMNLP 2021. We think it is not entirely fair to disregard our work, due to the two papers' very different contributions as well as their almost concurrent existence.  

*[1] Kottur, S., Moon, S., Geramifard, A., & Damavandi, B. (2021). SIMMC 2.0: A Task-oriented Dialog Dataset for Immersive Multimodal Conversations. In EMNLP.*

---

Moreover, as the discussion period is ending, we are also concerned whether the reviewer Sqbw has more feedback about our responses to prior concerns (#1, #2) so that we can improve our work and potentially its review evaluation?

replying_to: Replying to Multimodal Dialogue State Tracking
display_title: Official Review of Paper2639 by Reviewer SmCp

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper tackles the challenging task of multimodal dialogue state tracking. They synthesize a new dataset (DVD-DST) for the task based on previously proposed approaches. They propose VDTN, a multimodal model that jointly encodes video segments and text. It has two decoders: one to produce a new dialogue state in text format, and a visual decoder to reconstruct original video segments for self-supervised training. They test VDTN (and some baseline models) on DVD-DST and show its superiority. They provide several ablation studies to gain insight on what each component is contributing to the accuracy.
content.main_review:
Strengths:
- Overall I think it's a well-done paper. The task is relatively unexplored and it's nice to see new contributions. 
- The paper is well-written, tasks definitions are clear, and experiments seem reasonable.

Weaknesses:
- Experiments are on synthesized datasets. It's a well-known fact that testing on synthetic datasets result in overestimation of real performance and don't translate to real-world usability. Despite that, the state accuracy is only ~28%. I understand VDTN is supposed to be a baseline for future improvement, but how such low results on synthetic data are justified? I couldn't find any discussion on that in the paper.
- Another concern is the baseline models. None of those models are meant to be used for MM-DST. As authors have found, simply concatenating visual and textual embeddings don't perform well. Is it possible to compare to some of the multimodal models proposed over the years (e.g. [VilBERT](https://arxiv.org/abs/1908.02265), [SimVLM](https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.10904), [VLP](https://arxiv.org/abs/1909.11059), etc.)
- My last concern is the usefulness of the dataset. I find QA over videos an interesting concept with potentially a lot of use cases (finding a segment in a youtube video you're interested in) but the videos in this dataset are limited to only objects moving around. From current work, it's not clear how you can scale and what the limitations are. If I want to tackle a new domain, say videos of humans, what are the challenges besides defining new slots? I think a discussion on that in the paper would be interesting.
content.summary_of_the_review:
Overall I think this is a good paper taking a step in the right direction. 
I have a few concerns regarding the evaluation and the dataset mentioned above. As of now, I'm leaning towards a weak reject, but I'm willing to improve my score if those concerns are addressed.  

=========== UPDATE ===========
Thanks for your responses. My concerns regarding testing on synthetic datasets (instead of real crowdsourced data) and not comparing with previous multimodal models still remain. Thus I will keep my score.
Although I agree the task is hard, theoretically it should be possible to generate enough training data to cover all the paths objects can take. By evaluating on the same simulated data, you can possibly achieve close to 100% accuracy, while the current accuracy is far from that which makes me think either the data generation approach is not exhaustive enough, or the modeling is insufficient. With the current information in the paper, it's hard to tell.
Models such as UniVL (https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.06353) have Video and Language Pre-Training. I think a comparison with a truly multimodal model will shed more light on what components of the new models is benefiting the task.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper2639 by Reviewer SmCp

content.title: Response to Reviewer SmCp
content.comment:
We want to thank reviewer SmCp for the valuable and insightful feedback. We are delighted that the reviewer found our work a well-done paper, “taking a step in the right direction.” We are glad that the reviewer acknowledged the unexplored task and our new contributions. Please find below our response.

> Concern #1: “It's a well-known fact that testing on synthetic datasets result in overestimation of real performance and don't translate to real-world usability.” 
Thank you for your comment. 

We provide our response below and revise the paper in Appendix E.

We agree that the current state accuracy seems to be quite low at about 28%. However, we want to highlight that state accuracy is a very strict metric, which only considers a prediction as correct if it completely matches the ground truth. In DVD, assuming the average 10 objects per video with the set of attributes as in Figure 3 (+ ‘none’ value in each slot), we can roughly equate the multimodal DST as a 7200-class classification task, each class is a distinct set of objects, each with all possible attribute combinations.  Combined with the cascading error from object perception models, we think the current reported results of state accuracy are reasonable.

Moreover,  we want to highlight that the reported performance of baselines reasonably matches their own capacities in unimodal DST. First, we can consider Object State F1 as the performance on single-object state and it can closely correlate with the the joint state accuracy in unimodal DST (remember that unimodal DST such as MultiWOZ is only limited to a single object/entity per dialogue). As seen in Table 1, the Object state F1 results of TRADE, UniConv, and NADST are between 46-50%. This performance range is indeed not very far off from the performance of these baseline models in unimodal DST in the MultiWOZ benchmark. 

>Concern #2: “Is it possible to compare to some of the multimodal models proposed over the years (e.g. VilBERT, SimVLM, VLP, etc.)”

Thank you very much for your comment! We agree these models have achieved promising performance in other multimodal domains. If possible, we will extend them to the multimodal DST and report their results in our paper. 

>Concern #3: “If I want to tackle a new domain, say videos of humans, what are the challenges besides defining new slots?”

Thank you for your comment. We provide our response below and revise the paper in Appendix E.  

Say we want to scale to a new domain e.g. videos of humans, the first challenge from the current study is the recognition of human objects, which often have higher visual complexity than moving objects as in DVD. We also noted that it is impossible to define all human object classes as in CATER object classes, each of which is unique by its appearance. To overcome this limitation, we would want to explore multimodal DST with the research of human object tracking (e.g. [1]) and consider human object identities uniquely defined per video. Another limitation is the definition of slots to track in each human object. While this requires careful considerations, for both practical and ethical reasons, we noted several potential papers that investigate human attributes in dialogues such as human emotions [2]. Along these lines, we are excited to see interesting adaptations of multimodal dialogue states grounded on videos of humans. 

Finally, we also want to highlight that like other synthetic benchmarks such as CLEVR, we want to use DVD-DST in this work as a test bed to study and design better multimodal dialogue systems. However, we do not intend to use it to train practical systems. The DVD-DST benchmark should be used to supplement real-world video-grounded dialogue datasets.

*[1] Fernando, T., Denman, S., Sridharan, S., & Fookes, C. (2018). Tracking by prediction: A deep generative model for mutli-person localisation and tracking. In 2018 IEEE Winter Conference on Applications of Computer Vision (WACV).*

*[2] Wang, T., Hou, Y., Zhou, D., & Zhang, Q. (2021). A Contextual Attention Network for Multimodal Emotion Recognition in Conversation. In International Joint Conference on Neural Networks (IJCNN).*

replying_to: Replying to Response to Reviewer SmCp

content.title: Response to Reviewer SmCp (Concern #2)
content.comment:
We would like to add an additional response to reviewer SmCp’s Concern #2:

>Concern #2: “Is it possible to compare to some of the multimodal models proposed over the years (e.g. VilBERT, SimVLM, VLP, etc.)”

We tried to extend previous work that studies large pretrained transformer models such as VilBERT and VLP into our work. However, we noted that not all models are applicable in a generation-based setting such as VDTN (e.g. VilBERT is not ideal for generation-based tasks). Secondly, many models are focused on the image domain rather than the video domain. Specifically, in the video domain, we standardize to use both object-level and segment-level features for all baseline models in Table 1 (See Appendix C for training details). We expect that adapting prior multimodal pretrained models into this setup for MM-DST is not trivial and might be out of the scope of the paper.  

To make a fair comparison, instead, we recently conducted an experiment that combines VDTN with the GPT2 model [1]. We chose GPT2 as its language-model pretraining objective is suitable for a downstream generation task and the model is widely used in related research literature. While GPT2 was not prerained with a multimodal dataset, we still want to gauge the performance of VDTN+GPT2 as a baseline for future work of comparable scales. We added the results and revised our paper in Section 4 and Table 1. We briefly include the updated analysis below: 

We experimented with a version of VDTN in which the transformer network (Section 3.3) was initialized from a GPT2-base model with a pretrained checkpoint released by HuggingFace (https://huggingface.co/gpt2). Asides from using BPE to encode text sequences to match GPT2 embedding indices, we keep other components of the model the same. VDTN+GPT2 is about 36x bigger than our default VDTN model. As shown in Table 1, the performance gains of VDTN+GPT2 indicate the benefits of large-scale language models (LMs). Another benefit of using pretrained GPT2 is faster training time as we observed the VDTN+GPT2 converged much earlier than training it from scratch. From these observations, we are excited to see more future adaptation of large pretrained LMs or pretrained multimodal transformer models, in the MM-DST task.

| Model     | Object Detection F1  | Object Slot F1  | Object State F1 | Obj State  | MM State IoU@0.5 | MM State IoU@0.7 |
|-----------|----------------------|-----------------|-----------------|------------|------------------|------------------|
| VDTN      |                84.5% |           72.8% |           60.4% |      28.0% |            15.3% |            13.1% |
| VDTN+GPT2 |                85.2% |           76.4% |           63.7% |      30.4% |            16.8% |            14.3% |


*[1] Radford, A., Wu, J., Child, R., Luan, D., Amodei, D., & Sutskever, I. (2019). Language models are unsupervised multitask learners. OpenAI blog, 1(8), 9.*

replying_to: Replying to Multimodal Dialogue State Tracking
display_title: Official Review of Paper2639 by Reviewer NrrC

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper introduces a synthetic multi modal dialogue state tracking task where the task of the system is to talk to a user and answer questions describing a scene over multiple turns.  The introduce the task of multimodal dialogue state tracking, the synthetic dataset with dialogues and a transformer model which combines video and dialogue features to do answer user questions. 

They compare their network on their task and show that their method can keep track of the objects mentioned in the conversation better than baselines.
content.main_review:
The paper starts off with an ambitious goal of defining a new multi-modal task, a benchmark and a novel solution for it. But perhaps since it tries to do so much, it doesn't do any one of them particularly well. In the end you come out with a few vague ideas from the paper but nothing rigorous vs the alternatives. 

Strengths:
Since this paper defines a new task it has multiple novel ideas. The idea of doing multimodal dialogue state tracking, a dataset as a benchmark and a novel video + dialogue transformer model were new and interesting to me. 

Weaknesses:
Listing weaknesses by each of the contribution:
1) Multi-modal dialogue state tracking task definition: The authors only briefly define this in section 2. Considering that this would be a new class of tasks, I would like to see much more discussion on why the task was defined the way it was. Single start - end times with the objects themselves as slots. Perhaps the definition the authors describe was well suited for the synthetic task they settled on but there is no indication that such a representation is useful for a real world multi modal dialogue mentioned in Figure 6. 
Either this should have been clearly motivated by a real world task or there should be a detailed discussion of various ways in which the dialogue state could have been represented and why the one they chose is the best one. Simply proposing a paradigm without any pros and cons is not scientific research

2) Synthetic benchmark: Again here, for a new task it would be useful to know why the benchmark chosen (DVD) is the apt one. Looking at the dialogues generated in Table 12 and 13, its clear that the utterances are neither natural nor human comprehensible. Such a benchmark could still be useful but needs validation to show that it is indeed useful. Here also I would have liked to see more variation on the synthetic data generator instead of simply stating the default chosen. What happens if we trained on 130k dialogues instead?
Also stating that the released synthetic benchmark data-set has 13k dialogues which is larger than related DST benchmarks is wrong (appendix B) as its comparing apples to oranges

3) Video Dialogue transformer: The paper focuses a bunch of time showing that their Neural network indeed performs better than others on this task and contains the correct  ablation studies and relevant baselines but given the task is essentially visual reasoning, showing the performance on the prior benchmarks would be useful. 

Other comments: 
The paper only reports state accuracy but knowing the system answer accuracy would be interesting as well.
content.summary_of_the_review:
As stated due to the above concerns, the paper tries to do too many things and none of them well. It would be useful to break this into at least 2 more focused papers and show reasoning behind some of the chosen decisions. 


============= UPDATE ====================
Thank you for your responses. I think they take a step in the right direction. This comes back to my point that the contributions should be more thoroughly justified. 
My initial concerns regarding the formulation of the task and the choice of benchmarks still stand. In light of these responses, I'll revise my score to 5.

content.title: Response to Reviewer NrrC (part 1)
content.comment:
We want to thank reviewer NrrC for the valuable and detailed feedback. We are glad that the reviewer found our paper contains multiple novel and interesting ideas, including the introduction of MM-DST task and a video-dialogue transformer model. Please find below our response. 

> Concern #1: “Considering that this would be a new class of tasks, I would like to see much more discussion on why the task was defined the way it was.”: 

Thank you for your comments. We agree the current paper can be improved with a better discussion of the multimodal DST task. We revise the paper in Section 2 and briefly include our response below: 

**Our motivations**: 

Indeed, the introduction of the multimodal DST is motivated by our goal to extend dialogue agents to the real world, essentially to a spatio-temporal world where a dialogue agent can perceive, reason, and converse. In this task, ideally, we want a dialogue agent to possess a level of intelligence like a human counterpart. Several studies have analyzed how humans can perceive the world in visual context. [1,2] found that humans can recognize multiple visual objects and how their context, often embedded with other related objects, facilitates this capacity. 

Our work is more related to the recent study [3] which focuses on human capacity to create temporal stability across multiple objects. The study shows that some object features are carried over across memory episodes as a mechanism to maintain stable representations of objects over time. The multimodal DST task is designed to develop such capacities in multimodal dialogue systems. Specifically, we require systems to maintain a recurring information state of multiple objects, including their features, over a time period segmented by dialogue turns. While prior work has studied similar capacity in intelligent systems, they are mostly limited to vision-only or QA tasks but not in a dialogue task. Most closely related dialogue research work is [4] and [5]. However, [5] is limited to a single task-oriented object per dialogue, and [4] extends to multiple objects but does not require maintaining an information state with component slots for each object. Our work aims to address both limitations with a novel representation of multimodal dialogue state.

**The definition/representation of dialogue states**:

To this end, we proposed to extend conventional dialogue states. First, we use object identities themselves as a component of the dialogue state to account for the perception of multiple objects [1,2]. A dialogue state might have one or more objects and a dialogue system needs to update the object set as the dialogue carries on. Secondly, for each object, we define slots that represent the information state of objects in dialogues (defined by [3] as to-be-memorized “content” features of objects). The value of each slot is subject-specific and updated based on the dialogue context of the corresponding object. This definition of DST is closely based on the above well-studied human capacities while complementing the existing lines of dialogue research [4, 5]. 

One disadvantage of this representation is the assumption of a universal slot ontology, with a predefined set of slots. However, this limitation is not just limited to multimodal dialogues, but has been noted and addressed to some extent in unimodal DST [6]. We are excited to see similar future work targeting this challenge in multimodal DST. 

Another limitation of the current representation is the absence of temporal placement of objects in time. Naturally humans are able to associate objects and their temporal occurrence over a certain period. Similarly, in dialogue, we want the dialogue agent to achieve this capacity over the length of a conversation. Therefore, we defined two temporal-based slots for the start time and end time of the video segment that an object can be located by each dialogue turn.  In this work, we assume that a dialogue turn is limited to a single continuous time span. While this is a strong assumption, we believe it covers a large portion of natural conversational interactions.


*[1] Bar, M. (2004). Visual objects in context. Nature Reviews Neuroscience.*

*[2] Xu, Y., & Chun, M. M. (2009). Selecting and perceiving multiple visual objects. Trends in cognitive sciences.*

*[3] Fischer, C., Czoschke, S., Peters, B., Rahm, B., Kaiser, J., & Bledowski, C. (2020). Context information supports serial dependence of multiple visual objects across memory episodes. Nature communications.*

*[4] Pang, W., & Wang, X. (2020). Visual dialogue state tracking for question generation. In AAAI.*

*[5] Kottur, S., Moon, S., Geramifard, A., & Damavandi, B. (2021). SIMMC 2.0: A Task-oriented Dialog Dataset for Immersive Multimodal Conversations. In EMNLP.*

*[6] Rastogi, A., Zang, X., Sunkara, S., Gupta, R., & Khaitan, P. (2020). Towards scalable multi-domain conversational agents: The schema-guided dialogue dataset. In AAAI.*

content.title: Response to Reviewer NrrC (part 2)
content.comment:
> Concern #2: “For a new task it would be useful to know why the benchmark chosen (DVD) is the apt one.”

Thank you for your comments. We revised the paper in Section 4 ("DVD-DST benchmark") and briefly include our response below: 

Indeed, to study such multimodal DST tasks as defined in this paper, there are not many available suitable benchmarks. As mentioned in our response to Concern #1, the closest possible studies to our task are [1] and [2] but each contains its own shortfalls. In existing popular benchmarks of multimodal dialogues such as VisDial, we observe that a large number of data samples contain strong distribution bias in dialogue context, in which dialogue agents can simply ignore the whole dialogue and rely on image-only features  [3], or annotation bias, in which the causal link connecting dialogue history and current turn question is actually harmful [4]. These biases would obviate the need for a dialogue state in such benchmarks. 

We found that using DVD dialogues can address both biases. The dialogues are grounded on videos from CATER [5] which contain visually simple yet highly varied objects. The dialogues in DVD are synthetically designed with both short-term and long-term object references. These specifications remove the annotation bias in terms of object appearances in visual context and cross-turn dependencies in dialogue context. Moreover, as shown by our results in Table 1, models with access to videos only (RNN(V)) do not perform as well as models with access to dialogue only (RNN(D)). This indicates minimal distribution bias in dialogue context and models can generalize better by relying on dialogue features. 

We also want to highlight that like other synthetic benchmarks such as CLEVR in VQA, we want to use DVD in this work as a testbed to study and design better multimodal dialogue systems. We do not intend to use it to train practical systems for deployment. The DVD benchmark should be used to supplement real-world video-grounded dialogue datasets.

*[1] Pang, W., & Wang, X. (2020, April). Visual dialogue state tracking for question generation. In AAAI.*

*[2] Kottur, S., Moon, S., Geramifard, A., & Damavandi, B. (2021). SIMMC 2.0: A Task-oriented Dialog Dataset for Immersive Multimodal Conversations. In EMNLP.*

*[3] Kim, H., Tan, H., & Bansal, M. (2020, April). Modality-balanced models for visual dialogue. In AAAI.*

*[4] Qi, J., Niu, Y., Huang, J., & Zhang, H. (2020). Two causal principles for improving visual dialog. In CVPR.*

*[5] Girdhar, R., & Ramanan, D. (2020). CATER: A diagnostic dataset for Compositional Actions and TEmporal Reasoning. In ICLR.*

> Concern #3: “Given the task is essentially visual reasoning, showing the performance on the prior benchmarks would be useful.”

We would like to argue that the task is actually not essentially visual reasoning. As shown in our results in Table 1, the multimodal DST task relies strongly on dialogue contextual reasoning rather than visual reasoning. This can be seen through the results of RNN(D) vs. RNN(V) or Objects (random/all) vs. Q-retrieval. 

In addition, we would appreciate it if the reviewer can clarify on which specific “prior benchmarks” are referred to? 

>Concern #4: “The paper only reports state accuracy but knowing the system answer accuracy would be interesting as well.”

Thank you for your comment. We wondered about the same question and reported this experiment in Table 4. While the current results follow a naive integration of predicted states, the performance gains of response prediction show the benefits of a dialogue state in multimodal systems. As mentioned in Section 4 ("Impacts on downstream response prediction task"), more sophisticated methods from the image domain such as [1] can be adapted to fully exploit the decoded dialogue states. However, this is out of the scope of this paper and we are excited to see future work along this line.

*[1] Yi, K., Wu, J., Gan, C., Torralba, A., Kohli, P., & Tenenbaum, J. B. (2018). Neural-symbolic vqa: Disentangling reasoning from vision and language understanding. In NeurIPS.*
